Subject: LLM handoff — recommended access paths & next steps for NovusHealth

Hi Erin / Novus team —

Thanks again for the walkthrough this week. Per our call, I pulled together a short matrix (attached) that compares three viable ways to connect Novus’s VPCs/private DCs to a Redwood Private deployment: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink-style interface endpoints, and site-to-site (S2S) VPN tunnels. The sheet focuses on security posture, operational ownership, multi-region behavior, and unit-cost tradeoffs so you can pick the path that aligns with your compliance and latency needs.

Highlights up front:
- PrivateLink gives the tightest east-west isolation (no cross-account routing) and predictable egress IPs for allowlisting, but it has higher per-endpoint cost and can be fiddly for multi-region footprints.
- VPC Peering is simple and low-cost for same-account or permissive cross-account arrangements but increases blast radius and requires careful route table management for least-privilege.
- S2S VPN is the most flexible/cost-effective for multi-region or multi-cloud setups, but it adds network hop latency and requires robust monitoring and failover planning.

I've attached: llm_handoff_matrix.xlsx (decision matrix), redwood_network_diagram.png (example topology), and a one-pager that summarizes PrivateLink caveats.

Open questions I want to capture here so we can lock the recommendation:
1) Do you have strict egress IP allowlists for API callers (yes/no)?
2) Are there regulatory requirements that mandate vendor traffic be routed over a private link that the customer controls end-to-end?
3) Rough expected QPS and whether low single-digit-ms latency is critical for any flows.

If you like, we can propose a hybrid approach (control-plane on PrivateLink, data-plane over S2S with optional peering inside a security-approved VPC) so you get both predictable allowlisted endpoints and a cost-effective data path.

Next step: review matrix and pick 1–2 options to pilot. If Novus is comfortable, we can draft a mutual action plan and include the networking handoff checklist in the onboarding MOP.

Thanks — I’ll wait for your answers to the three questions and any notes from your security team.

Best,

Thanks Ben — useful summary and the matrix is helpful. A couple quick clarifications from our side:

1) Egress allowlisting: yes, our infra/security team requires a fixed set of egress IPs for the LLM inference endpoints used by our internal services. We can do CIDR blocks, but having static endpoints we can put into the allowlist is preferable.
2) Regulatory: we are in scope for multiple healthcare regulations. We need an auditable path where we can show that patient data never traverses public internet. PrivateLink sounds attractive here, but I’m unclear whether PrivateLink in multi-region setups means we need an endpoint per region or whether there’s an easier cross-region option.
3) QPS: initial pilot is low (hundreds of reqs/min) but we expect spikes during peak hours — latency sensitivity is moderate, but predictable p50/p95 is more important than absolute sub-ms.

I’m looping in our network/security lead (Samir) privately for any deep technical details — Samir, can you advise if Novus will accept a hybrid where control-plane/API calls are allowed via a PrivateLink endpoint and bulk payloads go over an encrypted S2S VPN?

—Erin

Ben / Erin — quick technical note from the infra side to help the decision:

- PrivateLink (interface endpoint) is the easiest way to get a predictable, allowlistable endpoint. For Novus’s use case (strict allowlist + auditability), PrivateLink fits very well because you can expose an interface endpoint in each region and you control who can attach. The tradeoff: you need one endpoint per region/az pair you want redundancy in, and there are AWS endpoint hourly + data processing costs.

- VPC Peering works well when both sides are in the same AWS account or you can accept cross-account peering. It does not provide a managed endpoint abstraction — traffic is routed via routes and security groups. That increases operational burden (route propagation, NAT considerations) and makes compliance audits slightly more complex because Novus will need to prove routing controls.

- S2S VPN is excellent when customers span on-prem and multiple public clouds. We typically see a ~15–40ms tail latency penalty depending on transit path, so if p95 latency matters, test it first. S2S also lets customers terminate in their network where they can apply packet inspection or DLP appliances (good for regulated traffic).

Operational recommendation for Novus:
1) Pilot with PrivateLink for API/control-plane traffic (predictable allowlist, easiest audit),
2) Use a pair of S2S tunnels for bulk data flows where cost matters and you can tolerate the small latency delta,
3) If Novus later wants to consolidate within AWS and move to same-account infra, consider migrating data-plane to VPC peering inside that dedicated VPC to reduce per-byte cost.

I added a short checklist to the shared drive (link above) for onboarding steps we need from Novus (account ids, preferred CIDRs for the RedTeam, contact for firewall rule changes).

Erin / Samir / Novus team — thanks for the quick responses and context. Based on your answers and Kimberly’s notes above, here’s a concise recommendation and proposed pilot plan: 

Recommendation (short):
- Control plane & API endpoints: PrivateLink in the primary region(s) Novus will use (predictable allowlists and audit records).
- Data plane (bulk payloads / model I/O): TLS-encrypted S2S VPN with dual tunnels for HA. This keeps per-byte costs lower and lets Novus route traffic through on-prem inspection devices if you need.
- Migration path: If at a later stage Novus consolidates into a same-account AWS VPC for production traffic, we can re-evaluate moving data-plane into a dedicated peering VPC to reduce egress fees.

Pilot plan (2–4 weeks):
1) Novus provides account IDs, preferred CIDR ranges to avoid overlap, and a contact for firewall rule updates (action: Erin).
2) Redwood creates PrivateLink endpoints in region A (and region B if you want geo-redundancy) and shares endpoint ENIs and required allowlist IPs.
3) Novus stand up two S2S tunnels to Redwood’s VPN concentrator (shared doc and sample terraform in the drive).
4) Run smoke tests (100–500 req/min) and capture p50/p95 latency and retransmits.
5) After acceptance, convert the pilot into a mutual action plan (MAP) with milestone dates and ownership.

Action items & owners:
- Erin: confirm account IDs, CIDRs, and whether region B should be included in pilot (due: Tue 2028-07-12).
- Samir: confirm whether Novus requires traffic inspection appliances in the data-plane path (due: Tue 2028-07-12).
- Kimberly: will provision the PrivateLink endpoints and hand off the topology doc.
- Ben/Marissa: will prepare the MAP draft and pricing for both PrivateLink+VPN pilot and the peering migration option.

If that looks good I’ll draft the MAP and the onboarding checklist and share for signatures.

Thanks —
